claim: Clarinet (cla-1) is a novel active zone gene in Caenorhabditis elegans.
source: In forward genetic screens, we isolated a novel Caenorhabditis elegans active zone gene, clarinet (cla-1).
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the abstract and supported by the forward genetic screen methodology described in the manuscript.

claim: cla-1 mutants exhibit defects in synaptic vesicle clustering.
source: cla-1 mutants exhibit defects in synaptic vesicle clustering, active zone structure and synapse number.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the abstract and supported by fluorescence microscopy data showing diffuse distribution of synaptic vesicle markers in cla-1 mutants.

claim: cla-1 mutants have reduced spontaneous vesicle release.
source: As a result, they have reduced spontaneous vesicle release and increased synaptic depression.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and supported by electrophysiology data showing reduced mini frequency in cla-1(S/M/L) mutants.

claim: cla-1 mutants show increased synaptic depression.
source: As a result, they have reduced spontaneous vesicle release and increased synaptic depression.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and supported by electrophysiology data showing enhanced depression during repeated stimulation.

claim: cla-1 mutants have fewer undocked vesicles contacting the dense projection.
source: cla-1 mutants show defects in vesicle distribution near the presynaptic dense projection, with fewer undocked vesicles contacting the dense projection and more docked vesicles at the plasma membrane.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and supported by electron microscopy quantification.

claim: cla-1 mutants have more docked vesicles at the plasma membrane.
source: cla-1 mutants show defects in vesicle distribution near the presynaptic dense projection, with fewer undocked vesicles contacting the dense projection and more docked vesicles at the plasma membrane.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and supported by electron microscopy data showing increased docked vesicles within 100 nm of the dense projection.

claim: cla-1 encodes three isoforms containing common C-terminal PDZ and C2 domains.
source: cla-1 encodes three isoforms containing common C-terminal PDZ and C2 domains with homology to vertebrate active zone proteins Piccolo and RIM.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and supported by sequence analysis and phylogenetic tree construction.

claim: CLA-1 PDZ and C2 domains have homology to vertebrate active zone proteins Piccolo and RIM.
source: cla-1 encodes three isoforms containing common C-terminal PDZ and C2 domains with homology to vertebrate active zone proteins Piccolo and RIM.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and supported by phylogenetic analysis showing the PDZ domain is most similar to RIM.

claim: The C-termini of all CLA-1 isoforms localize to the active zone.
source: The C-termini of all isoforms localize to the active zone.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and supported by imaging data showing C-terminally tagged CLA-1 colocalizes with active zone markers.

claim: The ~9000 amino acid long CLA-1L isoform is specifically required for vesicle clustering defects.
source: Specific loss of the ~9000 amino acid long isoform results in vesicle clustering defects and increased synaptic depression.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and supported by comparison of phenotypes between cla-1(L) and cla-1(S/M/L) alleles.

claim: Loss of the CLA-1L isoform results in increased synaptic depression.
source: Specific loss of the ~9000 amino acid long isoform results in vesicle clustering defects and increased synaptic depression.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and supported by electrophysiology data showing enhanced depression in cla-1(L) mutants.

claim: Active zone proteins cluster synaptic vesicles at presynaptic terminals.
source: Active zone proteins cluster synaptic vesicles at presynaptic terminals and coordinate their release.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: Active zone proteins coordinate synaptic vesicle release.
source: Active zone proteins cluster synaptic vesicles at presynaptic terminals and coordinate their release.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: The cytomatrix at the active zone is a protein dense region within the presynaptic bouton surrounded by synaptic vesicles.
source: This is achieved through the concerted action of conserved proteins that make up the cytomatrix at the active zone, a protein dense region within the presynaptic bouton that is surrounded by synaptic vesicles.
evidence: The claim is stated in the introduction and represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: Active zone proteins regulate neurotransmission by recruiting synaptic vesicles to the plasma membrane.
source: Active zone proteins regulate neurotransmission by recruiting synaptic vesicles to the plasma membrane, positioning calcium channels adjacent to the site of exocytosis, and priming synaptic vesicles for calcium-dependent release.
evidence: The claim is stated in the introduction and supported by citation to Südhof, 2012 and Ackermann et al., 2015.

claim: Active zone proteins position calcium channels adjacent to the site of exocytosis.
source: Active zone proteins regulate neurotransmission by recruiting synaptic vesicles to the plasma membrane, positioning calcium channels adjacent to the site of exocytosis, and priming synaptic vesicles for calcium-dependent release.
evidence: The claim is stated in the introduction and supported by citation to Südhof, 2012 and Ackermann et al., 2015.

claim: Active zone proteins prime synaptic vesicles for calcium-dependent release.
source: Active zone proteins regulate neurotransmission by recruiting synaptic vesicles to the plasma membrane, positioning calcium channels adjacent to the site of exocytosis, and priming synaptic vesicles for calcium-dependent release.
evidence: The claim is stated in the introduction and supported by citation to Südhof, 2012 and Ackermann et al., 2015.

claim: In vertebrates, the main active zone proteins that coordinate synaptic vesicle release are Liprin-α, RIM, RIM-BP, Elks and Munc-13.
source: In vertebrates, the main active zone proteins that coordinate synaptic vesicle release are Liprin-α, RIM, RIM-BP, Elks and Munc-13 (Südhof, 2012; Ackermann et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: Bassoon and Piccolo serve to cluster synaptic vesicles near the active zone.
source: Two additional proteins, Bassoon and Piccolo, serve to cluster synaptic vesicles near the active zone (Cases-Langhoff et al., 1996; Langnaese et al., 1996; Mukherjee et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: The core components of the active zone are conserved between vertebrates and invertebrates.
source: Although the core components of the active zone are conserved between vertebrates and invertebrates, Bassoon and Piccolo have long been considered exclusive to vertebrates.
evidence: The claim is stated in the introduction and represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: Bassoon and Piccolo have long been considered exclusive to vertebrates.
source: Although the core components of the active zone are conserved between vertebrates and invertebrates, Bassoon and Piccolo have long been considered exclusive to vertebrates.
evidence: The claim is stated in the introduction and represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: The N-terminus of Drosophila Bruchpilot (BRP) contains significant sequence homology to vertebrate ELKS.
source: While the N-terminus of Drosophila Bruchpilot (BRP) contains significant sequence homology to vertebrate ELKS (Wagh et al., 2006; Kittel et al., 2006), like Bassoon and Piccolo it also has a large C-terminal domain rich in coiled-coil structures that is thought to function in tethering synaptic vesicles (Matkovic et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: Drosophila BRP has a large C-terminal domain rich in coiled-coil structures that is thought to function in tethering synaptic vesicles.
source: While the N-terminus of Drosophila Bruchpilot (BRP) contains significant sequence homology to vertebrate ELKS (Wagh et al., 2006; Kittel et al., 2006), like Bassoon and Piccolo it also has a large C-terminal domain rich in coiled-coil structures that is thought to function in tethering synaptic vesicles (Matkovic et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is stated in the introduction and supported by citation.

claim: Drosophila Fife is a protein that contains ZnF, PDZ and C2 domains.
source: Recently, Drosophila Fife, a protein that contains ZnF, PDZ and C2 domains, was discovered based on sequence homology to the PDZ domain of vertebrate Piccolo, and shown to be an active zone protein (Bruckner et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is stated in the introduction and supported by citation.

claim: Drosophila Fife was discovered based on sequence homology to the PDZ domain of vertebrate Piccolo.
source: Recently, Drosophila Fife, a protein that contains ZnF, PDZ and C2 domains, was discovered based on sequence homology to the PDZ domain of vertebrate Piccolo, and shown to be an active zone protein (Bruckner et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is stated in the introduction and supported by citation.

claim: Drosophila Fife is an active zone protein.
source: Recently, Drosophila Fife, a protein that contains ZnF, PDZ and C2 domains, was discovered based on sequence homology to the PDZ domain of vertebrate Piccolo, and shown to be an active zone protein (Bruckner et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is stated in the introduction and supported by citation.

claim: Fife binds to and functionally interacts with Rim to dock synaptic vesicles.
source: Fife binds to and functionally interacts with Rim to dock synaptic vesicles and increase probability of release (Bruckner et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is stated in the introduction and supported by citation.

claim: Fife functionally interacts with Rim to increase probability of release.
source: Fife binds to and functionally interacts with Rim to dock synaptic vesicles and increase probability of release (Bruckner et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is stated in the introduction and supported by citation.

claim: No clear homologs of Piccolo, Bassoon, Fife, or of the coiled-coil domain of BRP have been identified for C. elegans.
source: No clear homologs of Piccolo, Bassoon, Fife, or of the coiled-coil domain of BRP have been identified for C. elegans.
evidence: The claim is stated in the introduction and represents the state of knowledge prior to this study.

claim: cla-1 null mutants exhibit reduced spontaneous synaptic vesicle release.
source: CLA-1 is required for normal synapse number and cla-1 null mutants exhibit reduced spontaneous synaptic vesicle release.
evidence: The claim is stated in the results introduction and supported by electrophysiology data.

claim: CLA-1 is required for normal synapse number.
source: CLA-1 is required for normal synapse number and cla-1 null mutants exhibit reduced spontaneous synaptic vesicle release.
evidence: The claim is stated in the results introduction and supported by synapse counting data.

claim: cla-1 mutants have a smaller dense projection.
source: Cla-1 mutants have a smaller dense projection and display defects in the clustering of the active zone protein SYD-2/Liprin-α.
evidence: The claim is stated in the results introduction and supported by electron microscopy measurements.

claim: cla-1 mutants display defects in the clustering of the active zone protein SYD-2/Liprin-α.
source: Cla-1 mutants have a smaller dense projection and display defects in the clustering of the active zone protein SYD-2/Liprin-α.
evidence: The claim is stated in the results introduction and supported by fluorescence microscopy data.

claim: cla-1 mutants exhibit a dramatic reduction in the number of synaptic vesicles contacting the dense projection.
source: They exhibit a dramatic reduction in the number of synaptic vesicles contacting the dense projection, and increased synaptic depression.
evidence: The claim is stated in the results introduction and supported by electron microscopy quantification.

claim: The cla-1 gene encodes three main isoforms (CLA-1L, CLA-1M and CLA-1S).
source: The cla-1 gene encodes three main isoforms (CLA-1L, CLA-1M and CLA-1S) containing PDZ and C2 domains with sequence homology to vertebrate Piccolo and RIM.
evidence: The claim is stated in the results introduction and supported by genomic and sequence analysis.

claim: All three CLA-1 isoforms share a C-terminal region that localizes to the active zone.
source: While all three isoforms share a C-terminal region that localizes to the active zone, their genetic requirement in synapse function and development differ
evidence: The claim is stated in the results introduction and supported by imaging data.

claim: The N-terminus of CLA-1L is specifically required for synaptic vesicle clustering.
source: the N-terminus of CLA-1L is specifically required for synaptic vesicle clustering and proper synaptic function during repeated stimulations
evidence: The claim is stated in the results introduction and supported by comparison of phenotypes between different alleles.

claim: The N-terminus of CLA-1L is required for proper synaptic function during repeated stimulations.
source: the N-terminus of CLA-1L is specifically required for synaptic vesicle clustering and proper synaptic function during repeated stimulations
evidence: The claim is stated in the results introduction and supported by electrophysiology data showing increased depression.

claim: The shorter CLA-1 isoforms or C-terminus are required for active zone assembly.
source: whereas the shorter isoforms or C-terminus are required for active zone assembly and proper synapse number.
evidence: The claim is stated in the results introduction and supported by comparison of phenotypes between different alleles.

claim: The shorter CLA-1 isoforms or C-terminus are required for proper synapse number.
source: whereas the shorter isoforms or C-terminus are required for active zone assembly and proper synapse number.
evidence: The claim is stated in the results introduction and supported by synapse counting data.

claim: cla-1(ola104) mutants exhibit diffuse distribution of the synaptic vesicle protein VMAT/CAT-1 compared to wild type controls.
source: From this screen, we identified allele ola104, which displayed a diffuse distribution of the synaptic vesicle protein VMAT/CAT-1 as compared to wild type controls (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by fluorescence microscopy images in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–D.

claim: In ola104 mutants, reduced intensity of synaptic puncta was accompanied by an increase in the extrasynaptic signal.
source: In ola104 mutants, reduced intensity of synaptic puncta was accompanied by an increase in the extrasynaptic signal, suggestive of a defect in synaptic vesicle clustering at the synapse.
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by fluorescence microscopy data.

claim: ola104 is a missense mutation in cla-1.
source: Using single-nucleotide polymorphism mapping, we identified ola104 as a missense mutation in cla-1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by SNP mapping data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: cla-1(ok560) phenocopied and failed to complement ola104.
source: An independent allele, cla-1(ok560), phenocopied and failed to complement ola104 (Figure 1C–F and Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by imaging data in the referenced figures.

claim: cla-1 is predicted to encode six isoforms of different lengths.
source: cla-1 is predicted to encode six isoforms of different lengths (Figure 1G).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by the genomic structure shown in Figure 1G.

claim: cla-1(ok560) results in a deletion of the promoter and part of the coding region of cla-1L.
source: cla-1(ok560) results in a deletion of the promoter and part of the coding region of cla-1L, and will be referred to henceforth as cla-1(L).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by genomic analysis.

claim: cla-1(wy1048) eliminates most of cla-1S and M, including the PDZ and C2 domains.
source: cla-1(wy1048), an allele we generated using CRISPR, eliminates most of cla-1S and M, including the PDZ and C2 domains.
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by CRISPR-based allele generation.

claim: cla-1(wy1048) is likely a null allele.
source: Because these domains are shared by all isoforms, this deletion is likely a null and the allele will henceforth be referred to as cla-1(S/M/L).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and based on inference from the deletion of shared domains.

claim: In cla-1(L) deletion mutants, the shorter isoforms are still expressed.
source: Importantly, in cla-1(L) deletion mutants, the shorter isoforms are still expressed, as evidenced by RT-PCR to the C-terminal PDZ domain (Figure 1—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1H.

claim: All cla-1 alleles examined showed defects in synaptic vesicle clustering in NSM.
source: Synaptic vesicle clustering was examined in five alleles affecting different isoforms (Figure 1G), and all alleles examined showed defects in synaptic vesicle clustering in NSM (Figure 1H).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by quantification shown in Figure 1H.

claim: CLA-1L may be specifically required for proper clustering of vesicles at the synapse.
source: Since the long-isoform-specific allele cla-1(L) exhibited as dramatic a defect as the null allele, we hypothesize that CLA-1L may thus be specifically required for proper clustering of vesicles at the synapse.
evidence: The claim is stated as a hypothesis based on comparison of phenotypes between alleles.

claim: CLA-1L is composed of approximately 9000 amino acids.
source: CLA-1L is composed of approximately 9000 amino acids and contains an extended repetitive region of about 4000 amino acids (Figure 1G).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by the protein structure shown in Figure 1G.

claim: CLA-1L contains an extended repetitive region of about 4000 amino acids.
source: CLA-1L is composed of approximately 9000 amino acids and contains an extended repetitive region of about 4000 amino acids (Figure 1G).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by the protein structure shown in Figure 1G.

claim: The 12 kb cDNA sequence encoding the repetitive region is comprised of tandem repeats, with a 282 bp repeat unit.
source: The 12 kb cDNA sequence encoding the repetitive region is comprised of tandem repeats, with a 282 bp repeat unit (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by sequence analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1G.

claim: The secondary structure of the repetitive region is predicted to consist of random coils interlaced with alpha helices.
source: The secondary structure of the repetitive region is predicted to consist of random coils interlaced with alpha helices.
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and based on computational prediction.

claim: CLA-1M is made up of ~3000 amino acids.
source: CLA-1M is made up of ~3000 amino acids, whereas CLA-1S is ~1000 amino acids long.
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and based on sequence analysis.

claim: CLA-1S is ~1000 amino acids long.
source: CLA-1M is made up of ~3000 amino acids, whereas CLA-1S is ~1000 amino acids long.
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and based on sequence analysis.

claim: The cla-1 PDZ domain is most similar to that of RIM.
source: Based on a phylogenetic analysis using the PDZ domain sequences, we found that the cla-1 PDZ domain is most similar to that of RIM, but constitutes a distinct clade (Figure 1I).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by the phylogenetic tree in Figure 1I.

claim: The cla-1 PDZ domain constitutes a distinct clade from RIM.
source: Based on a phylogenetic analysis using the PDZ domain sequences, we found that the cla-1 PDZ domain is most similar to that of RIM, but constitutes a distinct clade (Figure 1I).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by the phylogenetic tree in Figure 1I.

claim: cla-1 encodes a novel active zone protein.
source: This result, along with the lack of sequence homology between the rest of the CLA-1 protein (other than the C2 domains) and any known active zone proteins, suggests that cla-1 encodes a novel active zone protein.
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and based on phylogenetic analysis and lack of sequence homology.

claim: Each CLA-1 isoform is expressed broadly within the nervous system.
source: We found that each isoform is expressed broadly within the nervous system, as evidenced by a high degree of colocalization with an mCherry reporter under the pan-neuronal rab-3 promoter (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by imaging data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–C.

claim: CLA-1S was expressed broadly throughout the nervous system.
source: CLA-1S was expressed broadly throughout the nervous system, while CLA-1M and L were expressed in a subset of neurons.
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by promoter reporter analysis.

claim: CLA-1M and L were expressed in a subset of neurons.
source: CLA-1S was expressed broadly throughout the nervous system, while CLA-1M and L were expressed in a subset of neurons.
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by promoter reporter analysis.

claim: GFP::CLA-1L localizes to synapses at the developmental period in which the embryonic nervous system begins to form.
source: Using this strain, we determined that GFP::CLA-1L (homozygous endogenous) localizes to synapses at the developmental period in which the embryonic nervous system begins to form (three-fold stage: Figure 1—figure supplement 2D,E).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by imaging data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D,E.

claim: CLA-1L localized in a pattern reminiscent of synaptic vesicle marker RAB-3.
source: CLA-1L localized in a pattern reminiscent of synaptic vesicle marker RAB-3.
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by imaging data.

claim: CLA-1L colocalized with RAB-3 in NSM.
source: When we expressed mCherry::rab-3 cDNA under the NSM-specific promoter in the CRISPR strain, CLA-1L colocalized with RAB-3 in NSM (Figure 2A–C), indicating that CLA1L localizes to synapses, at or near synaptic vesicle clusters.
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by imaging data in Figure 2A–C.

claim: CLA-1L localizes to synapses, at or near synaptic vesicle clusters.
source: When we expressed mCherry::rab-3 cDNA under the NSM-specific promoter in the CRISPR strain, CLA-1L colocalized with RAB-3 in NSM (Figure 2A–C), indicating that CLA1L localizes to synapses, at or near synaptic vesicle clusters.
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and based on colocalization with RAB-3.

claim: Cell-specific expression of Cre in NSM leads to NSM-specific deletion of CLA-1L.
source: However, cell-specific expression of Cre in NSM, which leads to NSM-specific deletion of CLA-1L, resulted in the cla-1L mutant phenotype in NSM.
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and based on the CRISPR-Cre strategy described.

claim: Cell-specific deletion of CLA-1L in NSM resulted in diffuse distribution of synaptic vesicle proteins in NSM.
source: However, cell-specific expression of Cre in NSM, which leads to NSM-specific deletion of CLA-1L, resulted in the cla-1L mutant phenotype in NSM. Namely, we observed a diffuse distribution of synaptic vesicle proteins in NSM (Figure 2F and G).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by imaging data in Figure 2F and G.

claim: CLA-1L is required in NSM for synaptic vesicle clustering.
source: These findings indicate that CLA-1L is required in NSM for synaptic vesicle clustering and are consistent with it acting cell-autonomously in NSM.
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and based on cell-specific deletion experiments.

claim: CLA-1L acts cell-autonomously in NSM.
source: These findings indicate that CLA-1L is required in NSM for synaptic vesicle clustering and are consistent with it acting cell-autonomously in NSM.
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and based on cell-specific deletion and rescue experiments.

claim: Cell-specific expression of CLA-1L in NSM rescued the synaptic vesicle phenotype in NSM.
source: In those animals, the resulting GFP::CLA-1L localized in a synaptic pattern in the NSM process (Figure 2M, arrow), colocalized with the synaptic vesicle marker RAB-3 (Figure 2K–M), and rescued the synaptic vesicle phenotype in NSM (Figure 2L, arrow, and N).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by imaging data in Figure 2K–N.

claim: CLA-1L is both necessary and sufficient to mediate synaptic vesicle clustering in NSM.
source: Our findings indicate that CLA-1L is required cell-autonomously in the NSM neuron, where it is both necessary and sufficient to mediate synaptic vesicle clustering.
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and based on cell-specific deletion and rescue experiments.

claim: cla-1(L) mutants exhibited diffuse synaptic vesicle patterns in the AIY interneuron.
source: We found that cla-1(L) mutants exhibited diffuse synaptic vesicle patterns in the AIY interneuron (Figure 3A–D) and the PVD mechanosensory neuron (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–C)
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by imaging data in Figure 3A–D.

claim: cla-1(L) mutants exhibited diffuse synaptic vesicle patterns in the PVD mechanosensory neuron.
source: We found that cla-1(L) mutants exhibited diffuse synaptic vesicle patterns in the AIY interneuron (Figure 3A–D) and the PVD mechanosensory neuron (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–C)
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by imaging data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–C.

claim: cla-1(L) mutants did not exhibit diffuse synaptic vesicle patterns in GABAergic or cholinergic motor neurons that innervate body wall muscles.
source: but not the GABAergic or cholinergic motor neurons that innervate body wall muscles (Figure 3E–I and L; Figure 3—figure supplement 1D–F)
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by imaging data in the referenced figures.

claim: CLA-1L is required for synaptic vesicle clustering at specific synapses in C. elegans.
source: These data demonstrate that CLA-1L is required for synaptic vesicle clustering at specific synapses in C. elegans, indicating that the molecular mechanisms for vesicle clustering may be cell (or synapse) specific.
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and based on differential phenotypes in different neuron types.

claim: The molecular mechanisms for vesicle clustering may be cell (or synapse) specific.
source: These data demonstrate that CLA-1L is required for synaptic vesicle clustering at specific synapses in C. elegans, indicating that the molecular mechanisms for vesicle clustering may be cell (or synapse) specific.
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and based on inference from differential phenotypes.

claim: Both cla-1L(L) and cla-1(S/M/L) mutants exhibited resistance to aldicarb.
source: Both cla-1L(L) and cla-1(S/M/L) mutants exhibited resistance to aldicarb, suggesting compromised synaptic transmission (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by aldicarb assay data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: cla-1 (S/M/L) animals were more resistant to aldicarb than cla-1L(L).
source: cla-1 (S/M/L) animals were more resistant to aldicarb than cla-1L(L) (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A), suggesting that while the long isoform plays a role in synaptic transmission, the shorter isoforms and/or the C-terminus might execute additional functions that affect synaptic vesicle release.
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by aldicarb assay data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The shorter CLA-1 isoforms and/or the C-terminus might execute additional functions that affect synaptic vesicle release.
source: cla-1 (S/M/L) animals were more resistant to aldicarb than cla-1L(L) (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A), suggesting that while the long isoform plays a role in synaptic transmission, the shorter isoforms and/or the C-terminus might execute additional functions that affect synaptic vesicle release.
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and based on inference from differential aldicarb resistance.

claim: The frequency of spontaneous postsynaptic currents was reduced by 46% in cla-1(S/M/L) mutants.
source: In cla-1(S/M/L), but not in cla-1(L) mutants, the frequency of spontaneous postsynaptic currents ('minis') was reduced by 46% (Figure 6A,C).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by electrophysiology data in Figure 6A,C.

claim: Mini amplitude was unchanged in cla-1 mutants.
source: Mini amplitude was unchanged (Figure 6D), indicating that postsynaptic receptor function was not perturbed.
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by electrophysiology data in Figure 6D.

claim: Postsynaptic receptor function was not perturbed in cla-1 mutants.
source: Mini amplitude was unchanged (Figure 6D), indicating that postsynaptic receptor function was not perturbed.
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and based on inference from unchanged mini amplitude.

claim: Evoked response to a single presynaptic depolarization was unchanged in cla-1 mutants.
source: While evoked response to a single presynaptic depolarization was unchanged in cla-1 mutants (Figure 6B,E), subsequent release during a 20 Hz stimulation train was impaired (Figure 6F and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by electrophysiology data in Figure 6B,E.

claim: Subsequent release during a 20 Hz stimulation train was impaired in cla-1 mutants.
source: While evoked response to a single presynaptic depolarization was unchanged in cla-1 mutants (Figure 6B,E), subsequent release during a 20 Hz stimulation train was impaired (Figure 6F and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by electrophysiology data in Figure 6F and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: An increase in depression upon repeated stimulation indicates a defect in the number of vesicles that can be readily recruited by depolarization.
source: An increase in depression upon repeated stimulation indicates a defect in the number of vesicles that can be readily recruited by depolarization, and might be a functional consequence of the reduced number of vesicles contacting the dense projection (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and represents an interpretation of the electrophysiology data.

claim: The long isoform of CLA-1 might be solely responsible for synaptic vesicle recruitment to sustain release upon repetitive stimulation.
source: Our findings therefore suggest that the long isoform of CLA-1 might be solely responsible for synaptic vesicle recruitment to sustain release upon repetitive stimulation.
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and based on inference from electrophysiology data.

claim: cla-1(S/M/L);unc-10/rim double mutants showed reduced evoked release in response to a single stimulus when compared to unc-10/rim mutants alone.
source: We found that cla-1(S/M/L);unc-10/rim double mutants showed reduced evoked release in response to a single stimulus when compared to unc-10/rim mutants alone (Figure 6E).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by electrophysiology data in Figure 6E.

claim: CLA-1S was greatly reduced, but not completely absent, in unc-104/Kinesin-3 mutants.
source: We found that CLA-1S was greatly reduced, but not completely absent, in unc-104/Kinesin-3 mutants (Figure 7A,C), consistent with previous studies showing down-regulation of active zone proteins in Drosophila kinesin-3 mutants (Pack-Chung et al., 2007; Li et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by imaging data in Figure 7A,C.

claim: CLA-1S was completely absent from the axon in mutants for the active zone scaffold protein SYD-2/Liprin-α.
source: Strikingly, CLA-1S was completely absent from the axon in mutants for the active zone scaffold protein SYD-2/Liprin-α, and greatly reduced in mutants for syd-1/mSYD1A (Figure 7A,C).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by imaging data in Figure 7A,C.

claim: CLA-1S was greatly reduced in mutants for syd-1/mSYD1A.
source: Strikingly, CLA-1S was completely absent from the axon in mutants for the active zone scaffold protein SYD-2/Liprin-α, and greatly reduced in mutants for syd-1/mSYD1A (Figure 7A,C).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by imaging data in Figure 7A,C.

claim: syd-2/Liprin-α mutants have a profound defect in synaptic vesicle accumulation.
source: syd-2/Liprin-α mutants have a profound defect in synaptic vesicle accumulation (Zhen and Jin, 1999; Patel et al., 2006; Stigloher et al., 2011)
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by citations.

claim: Double mutants of cla-1 and syd-2 did not show a detectable enhanced synaptic phenotype.
